title: School visits to Maple Ridge Heritage Farm
context: You will hear an education officer giving information to teachers who are planning school trips to a heritage farm.

lines.t: Good morning, and thanks for joining this briefing for teachers and group leaders who are bringing classes to Maple Ridge Heritage Farm this spring. I'm Kevin, the education officer here, and I'll explain how the day works and what activities are available.

First, a little background. Maple Ridge was run by the Hartley family for more than a hundred years. When the last member of the family retired, the city council looked into buying the land, but they decided it would be too expensive. In the end the farm was taken over by a charity, the Rural Heritage Trust, which still runs it today. So any money you spend here goes straight back into the farm.

Now, arrival times. Our gates open at nine, but between nine and nine thirty our staff are busy feeding the animals, so please don't arrive then. Equally, if you come much after ten, you'll struggle to fit everything in. So please aim to arrive between nine thirty and ten.

Lunch. On a fine day, groups eat at the picnic tables beside the pond. If it rains, a lot of teachers assume they can use the visitor centre, but that's only for café customers, and it gets very crowded. Instead, we open up the big red barn, which has plenty of room for several classes. Please don't plan to eat on your buses, because most drivers won't allow it.

The children can get really close to the animals here. They're welcome to stroke and feed the goats and the rabbits, and the sheep too. The one exception is the horses. They're gentle most of the time, but they can kick if they're surprised, so children mustn't touch them.

As for cost, it's twelve dollars per child, and teachers come free. Lunch isn't included, so children should bring a packed lunch. What is included is a worksheet pack, which we'll email to you a week before your visit, so you can prepare the class. Some schools ask about souvenirs, and there is a gift shop, but nothing is included in the price.

Okay, now the activities. None of these needs to be booked in advance. You just sign up at the information desk when you arrive. First, sheep shearing. This only takes place in the mornings, because in the afternoon it gets too warm for the sheep, so do that one first if you can.

Pond dipping is always popular. The children use nets to catch tiny creatures and look at them under a magnifying glass. It's very safe, but the edges of the pond are muddy, so children have to wear boots. If anyone forgets, we have a few spare pairs.

Then there's the tractor ride, which takes about twenty minutes and goes all round the farm. The ride costs an extra two dollars per child, because of the fuel. Even very young children can go on it, as long as they sit next to an adult.
In the old dairy, children can try cheese making. The dairy's quite a small building, so we can only take fifteen children at a time. If your class is bigger, we'll split it into two groups.
And finally, the maze. It's made from tall hedges and it's great fun, but it's very easy to get lost, so we don't allow children under five to go in. Older children love it.

I should just mention that the hay bale slide, which some of you may remember from last year, is closed this season while we build a new one. Right, I'll send all of this to you in an email, and if you have any questions, please get in touch.
